about: Peak isometric strength per joint motor: [against the joint's positive direction, along it], N m for hinges, N for the shoulder girdle's slides. Each hinge motor's strength at any moment is its peak scaled by its curve in `curves`, by angle and speed. source: study | proposed.

curves.about: Strength by joint angle and speed, as a fraction of the peak in `joints` (moonshot/body/skeleton.py strength_curves and StrengthCurve; the controller caps each motor at it every step). Per strength key and direction (`against` / `along` the joint's positive direction, as `max`; angles anatomical, moonshot/motion/kinematics.py): `torque_nm` [speed][angle], a measured surface normalised to its own isometric maximum; or `torque_nm` [angle], isometric torque by angle normalised to its maximum, times its own `speed` scale or else the `speed` default; else flat in angle, with the `speed` default. A key or direction with no curve says why in its `reason`. `grip_by_wrist` scales the long finger flexors by wrist flexion. Speeds are shortening, the joint moving the way the motor pushes; off the grid each holds its nearest edge. Slides (pelvis, girdle) have no curve.

speed.reason: Every hinge without its own surface: the elbow's mid-range decay from Frey-Law et al. 2012 (J Appl Biomech 28(6):726-737, men, at 65 deg: flexion 63.0 / 44.7 / 38.7 / 33.1 / 27.9 / 25.7 N m and extension 52.8 / 39.6 / 35.6 / 31.8 / 26.1 / 24.6 N m at 0-300 deg/s, each normalised and the two averaged), mid-range being where the decay is least. The authors found every joint and direction differs, so this stands in until each has its own

lengthening.reason: A motor being stretched (moving against its push) keeps its isometric strength. People's eccentric strength is somewhat higher; keeping it at isometric errs weak

along.reason: Flexion: Frey-Law et al. 2012, J Appl Biomech 28(6):726-737, Table 4, men's mean peak torque (Biodex, 30 men) by elbow flexion and speed. Three cells are proposed, where over half the men couldn't reach the speed: 240 deg/s at 15 deg (28.1) and 300 deg/s at 15 and 40 deg (24.1, 26.1), each extrapolated along speed from its two fastest measured cells

against.reason: Extension: Frey-Law et al. 2012, Table 5, men's mean peak torque by elbow flexion and speed. Two cells are proposed, where over half the men couldn't reach the speed: 240 and 300 deg/s at 110 deg (27.9, 25.0), extrapolated along speed from its two fastest measured cells

along.reason: Raising the arm: Aronis et al. 2025, J Funct Morphol Kinesiol 11(1):20, Table 1, 14 men standing, mean isometric shoulder flexion torque by elevation (the 77 N m peak in `joints` is its 90 deg value). Proposed below 90 deg, where it holds its 90 deg value: Koski & McGill 1994 (Clin Biomech 9(2):99-104, 26 men, seated) measured 89.9 N m at 0 deg and 68.6 at 45 deg, on another rig and cohort, so no shape joins the two

speed.reason: Koski & McGill 1994, 26 men: concentric shoulder flexion at 50 deg/s 46.9 N m against 68.6 isometric, both at 45 deg (0.684). Proposed past 50 deg/s, which nobody measured: the `speed` default's decay scaled through that point

against.reason: Lowering the arm (extension, adduction): no men's torque by elevation angle found in the open literature (Otis et al. 1990, Am J Sports Med 18(2):119-123, measured flexion, abduction and the rotations; Mayer et al. 1994, Int J Sports Med 15 Suppl 1:S19-25, give men's shoulder extension by speed and its angle of peak torque, paywalled). Flat, with the `speed` default

along.reason: Internal rotation (+): Ruas et al. 2015, Sports 3(3):236-245, Table 2, 20 men supine with the arm abducted 90 deg, preferred arm, concentric at 60 deg/s, mean torque every 10 deg from 80 deg external (-80) to 50 deg internal rotation: strongest stretched. Proposed: that 60 deg/s shape stands in for the isometric one, at every speed (the `speed` default) and every elevation of the arm (Baptista de Oliveira Medeiros et al. 2026, Shoulder Elbow, review: the curves depend on arm position)

against.reason: External rotation: Ruas et al. 2015, Table 2, as internal rotation: strongest mid-range, weakest rotated fully out. Proposed as for internal rotation

sh_plane.reason: The plane of elevation (horizontal adduction +, abduction -): no men's torque by this angle found in the open literature. Flat, with the `speed` default

pron.reason: Forearm rotation by its angle: people pronate hardest with the forearm supinated and supinate hardest with it pronated, each weakest at its own end of the range (Matsuoka et al. 2006, J Hand Surg Am 31(5):801-805, 51 adults; Gordon et al. 2004, J Orthop Res 22(1):208-213; for supination also O'Sullivan & Gallwey 2002, J Electromyogr Kinesiol 12(4):275-285, 24 men), but the per-angle numbers are paywalled, as are Xia & Frey-Law 2015's pronation-supination torque-angle-velocity envelopes (Int J Hum Factors Model Simul 5(1):33-52). Flat, with the `speed` default

along.reason: Flexion: Behrens et al. 2019, Front Bioeng Biotechnol 7:181, Table 1, 18 men, mean isometric wrist flexion torque at 30 deg extension, neutral and 30 deg flexion (fingers flexed round a handle); Delp et al. 1996 (J Biomech 29(10):1371-1375, 10 men) found the flexion moment peaking at 40 deg flexion. Proposed: past 30 deg either way it holds its ends; the `speed` default (Xia & Frey-Law 2015 measured wrist torque to 240 deg/s; paywalled)

against.reason: Extension: Delp et al. 1996, 10 men: the extension moment was relatively constant from 30 deg flexion to 70 deg extension (its 7.1 N m mean peak is the one in `joints`), so flat. Proposed: the `speed` default, as for flexion

wr_dev.reason: Radial and ulnar deviation by angle: Delp et al. 1996 measured it in 10 men, but the abstract gives only the peaks (in `joints`) and the article is paywalled. Flat, with the `speed` default

trunk_flex.reason: Frey-Law's lab measured men's trunk surfaces (Stockdale 2011, MS thesis, University of Iowa, 15 men: flexion strongest upright, extension strongest at 40 deg flexion, both falling with speed), unreviewed and only as figures; Keller & Roy 2002 (J Spinal Disord Tech 15(4):312-318, 10 men, 10 women) found flexion strongest at 20-30 deg and extension at 50 deg flexion, the numbers paywalled. Flat, with the `speed` default

trunk_lat.reason: Huang & Thorstensson 2000 (Eur J Appl Physiol 83(6):573-577, 12 men): isometric lateral flexion 80-172 N m within 20 deg either side, strongest bent 11-15 deg the other way, concentric torque falling with speed; the per-angle numbers are paywalled. Flat, with the `speed` default

trunk_rot.reason: Axial rotation by angle: only Stockdale 2011 (MS thesis, as trunk_flex: men strongest at 30 deg rotation, 71.3 N m), unreviewed and only as figures. Flat, with the `speed` default

hand.reason: No men's torque by finger-joint angle found for these joints; the long flexors' dependence on the wrist is `grip_by_wrist`. Flat, with the `speed` default

grip_by_wrist.reason: Finger flexion (the long flexors cross the wrist) by wrist flexion (+) / extension (-): strongest at 35 deg extension and 0.71 at 15 deg extension (O'Driscoll et al. 1992, J Hand Surg Am 17(1):169-177: two thirds to three quarters); 0.50 at 30 deg flexion (Bhardwaj et al. 2011, Indian J Plast Surg 44(1):55-58, 100 adults, splinted: 13.9 kg against 27.9 kg at 45 deg extension, the strongest splinted position). Proposed: 1.0 past 45 deg extension, where neither measured, and 0.27 at full flexion, the 15 deg extension to 30 deg flexion slope continued

hand_stiffness_nm_per_rad.reason: Finger servo stiffness from trainual's accepted vise take (sim/build_scene.py KP): fingers are compliant, and with grip effort's co-contraction this gives the 11-14 N grip the lifting studies give for the 0.8 kg blank. Arm joints instead reach full strength 5 deg off target

body_stiffness.reason: Servo stiffness, N m/rad for hinges and N/m for slides. People's arms are compliant: passive shoulder-elbow stiffness is ~10.8 / 8.7 N m/rad (Frank et al. 2013, from earlier work) and rises with co-contraction when holding posture (Franklin & Milner 2003). The controller's feedforward does the moving; stiffness only corrects disturbances, and a stiff arm squeezes a pinched part out of the grip

pelvis_x.reason: The legs' push on the pelvis, far above what a weight shift needs

pelvis_z.reason: As pelvis_x; also carries the upper body's weight

trunk_flex.reason: Trunk flexion/extension strength well above the ~30 N m it costs to hold a 20 deg lean

trunk_rot.reason: Axial trunk rotation, the weakest trunk direction

sh_plane.reason: Harbo et al. 2012 (178 healthy adults): men's shoulder abduction ~60, adduction ~83 N m

sh_elev.reason: Standing isometric shoulder flexion, adult men: ~77 N m at 90 deg elevation (PMC12821543)

elbow.reason: Harbo et al. 2012, men: elbow extension ~47, flexion ~51 N m

pron.reason: Supination ~6.3, pronation ~5.2 N m (1987 data cited in J Hand Surg forearm-torque normative study)

wr_flex.reason: Wrist, 10 healthy men: extension 7.1, flexion 12.2 N m

wr_dev.reason: Wrist, 10 healthy men: ulnar 9.5, radial 11.0 N m

mcp_flex.reason: Tip pinch ~80-93 N in young men (Mathiowetz 1985; Iranian norms) at ~55 mm from the MCP

mcp_abd.reason: Interossei, a small fraction of flexion

pip.reason: Tip pinch ~80 N at ~40 mm from the PIP

dip.reason: Tip pinch ~80 N at ~20 mm from the DIP

thumb_cmc_flex.reason: Key pinch ~113-116 N in young men (Mathiowetz 1985; Iranian norms) at ~45 mm

thumb_mcp_flex.reason: Key pinch at ~30 mm from the MCP

thumb_ip.reason: Key pinch at ~15 mm from the IP
